title: The safety model

headings.text: Ownership and borrowing without a borrow checker

text: Zark is a systems language, so it cannot promise what a garbage-collected language promises. It makes a narrower, honest promise: a mistake is stopped as early as the compiler can see it, and otherwise it is stopped loudly, with a file and a line, instead of corrupting memory in silence. This page lists every case, so you know what you can lean on. # Build modes Mode How Checks Use it for safe zark run , zark build everything below development, tests, most programs safe and optimized -O the same checks, optimized by LLVM production when you want the checks to stay unchecked --release bounds, division, overflow and null checks removed a program that you have already run through the safe modes bare metal --freestanding no runtime helpers, so no checks kernels and drivers Compile-time checks (types, ownership, escapes) are the same in all modes. The difference is only what is checked while the program runs. # The three outcomes Every problem ends in exactly one of three ways. A compile error. The program is not built. This is the best outcome. A panic. The program stops at once with a message, a file and a line ( panic: index 3 out of bounds (len 3) at main.zk:4 ). A panic means a bug in the program, and it cannot be caught. An error value. A function returns !T and the caller decides. This is for things that can go wrong in a correct program: no file, bad input, no memory. # What is stopped, and when Mistake What happens Wrong type, lossy conversion, missing as compile error Number literal outside its type ( u8 x = 300 ) compile error Assigning to a const compile error Dropping an !T result compile error A match that produces a value and misses a variant compile error A forgotten variant in a match statement nothing happens (statements may skip variants) A struct that contains itself, an alias cycle, an infinitely growing generic compile error Using a variable after free , destroy , deinit , close or join compile error Freeing the same variable twice compile error Returning or storing a pointer or slice into a local compile error Using a pointer or slice into a List or Map after it changed compile error Changing a List or Map inside a loop that iterates over it (and goes on to the next round) compile error A Thread that is not joined on every path, dropped, or returned together with a local it captured compile error comptime assertion that is false compile error Index or slice out of bounds panic Integer division or remainder by zero, or MIN / -1 panic Integer overflow in + , - , * panic Out of memory, bad input, a missing file error value A List that was never given an allocator error value ( error.NoAllocator ) A float that does not fit an integer ( 1e30 as i32 ) saturates to the nearest limit, nan becomes 0 A shift by too many bits the count is masked to the width of the type Reading a variable that was never assigned not possible: variables start as zero Dereferencing null , or running out of stack by endless recursion the program stops with a clear message and a backtrace Nothing in the list is undefined behavior in the safe mode. The same program gives the same result with the native backend, with --llvm and with -O , and a test in the repository keeps it that way. # Ownership and borrowing without a borrow checker Zark does not have lifetimes or a borrow checker as Rust has. It has something smaller that you can learn in ten minutes, and that catches the mistakes that happen in practice. It follows variables inside one function : A parameter or method marked move takes the value over. The standard library marks free , destroy , every deinit , join , and the close of sockets and streams. After the call, the variable is dead until you assign it again. A method marked borrows returns a pointer or slice into the object ( List.at , List.slice , Map.get_ptr ). A method marked invalidates may move the memory ( push , put , insert ). If you call an invalidates method, every pointer or slice you took from that object earlier is dead. A pointer or slice to a local array or struct cannot leave the function: not by return and not by being stored through a pointer parameter or into a global. A loop that iterates over a container ( for (auto x : list) , list.slice() , this- items ) cannot call an invalidates method on it and then go on to the next round. Leave with break or return right after the change, or iterate over a copy. A struct declared owned (in the standard library, Thread ) must be consumed in every scope it lives in: joined, detached, passed on, or returned. This includes the exits taken by ? , so write defer t.join(); or errdefer t.join(); right after creating it. Dropping such a value on the spot is refused. The state is followed through if , match , catch , loops, defer and errdefer . The checker is deliberately conservative where it would otherwise reject valid programs, so it says nothing about what it cannot see. Four things it does not see: Copies. auto q = p; a.destroy(p); use(q) is not caught. Fields for move . a.free(this- data) does not mark the field as freed. (Borrows and invalidates do follow field paths such as this- items .) Other functions. A function that frees what you passed to it, without being marked move , is invisible. Data races. Nothing checks that two threads do not touch the same memory. You can mark your own functions with the same words, and the check then covers them too. See memory . # Closing the gap with tools What the compiler cannot prove, a tool can catch while you test. DebugAllocator gives every block its own pages and makes a freed block inaccessible. A use after free, even through a copy of the pointer, stops at the exact access with the block's number, and deinit() lists everything that was never freed. Output exit code 1 Output exit code 1 Run your tests with a DebugAllocator as the allocator. Because functions receive the allocator as a parameter, no code needs to change to do it. zark test runs every test block. -g adds line and varia

title: Writing idiomatic Zark

headings.text: A type that owns memory: init, deinit, errdefer
Pass the allocator, choose the lifetime
Errors: name them and keep them
Model the data with unions and enums
Let the zero value be useful

text: The language lets you write a program in many ways. This page shows the way that works with the compiler's checks instead of against them, and that other Zark programmers will recognize. Every example here compiles and runs. # Names and layout Types are PascalCase , functions, methods, variables and fields are snake_case , constants are UPPER_CASE . Files are snake_case.zk . A function that builds a value is called init or new (and is static ), and a function that releases it is deinit . Put the types and functions that go together in one file, and import it with as when the names might collide ( modules ). # A type that owns memory: init , deinit , errdefer The pattern is always the same: the constructor takes the allocator, remembers it, and cleans up after itself if a later step fails. The destructor is marked move , so using the value afterwards does not compile. Output Notice three things. The buffer stores the allocator it was created with, so deinit needs no argument and cannot free with the wrong one. text() is marked borrows : a caller that keeps the result and then changes the buffer is told about it. A caller that forgets deinit is caught by the DebugAllocator in tests. When a constructor has several steps, each step that allocates gets an errdefer that undoes it. It runs only if the function returns an error: Output If the second allocation fails, the first is freed on the way out. If both succeed, errdefer does nothing and the caller owns both. # Pass the allocator, choose the lifetime A function that allocates takes an Allocator as its first parameter. It does not choose where memory comes from, so the caller can give it an arena, a fixed buffer or a debugging allocator. Group things that live and die together in one arena. A request, a frame, a compile unit, a test: one arena, one defer arena.deinit() . Output split_words never frees anything: the result is a slice into the arena's memory, and the arena releases it all at once. Compare with a function that returned a List that the caller had to remember to deinit . # Take slices, return values For input, take the most general view of the data: str instead of a list of characters, T[] instead of a List T . The function then works with arrays, lists, and parts of both, and it cannot reallocate what it was given. Output For output, return small values and structs by value. Use an out-parameter only for something big that already exists (a buffer to fill). # Errors: name them and keep them Return a named error from the place that understands the problem. Pass errors up with ? where you cannot do better, and convert them with catch only at the place that knows what to do. Output exit code 1 main returns !void , so an unhandled error becomes the exit message of the program, as the last line shows. Do not use catch 0 to silence an error unless a zero is really the right answer. Use ?T for there may be nothing and !T for it may fail . A lookup that finds nothing is not an error: Output # Model the data with unions and enums Make impossible states impossible. A request that is either waiting, running with a progress, or done with a result is a union, not three booleans: Output When you add a variant, every match that produces a value and has no _ arm stops compiling until you handle it. That is the compiler working as a checklist, so prefer this form to a match statement when a forgotten case would be a bug (a statement may skip variants without a word). Avoid _ = arms in a match over your own types: they hide exactly this help. # Let the zero value be useful A struct literal sets what you name and zeroes the rest, and variables start as zero. Design a type so that the all-zero value is a valid, empty one, and you need no constructor and no flag for initialized : Output Types with an allocator are the exception: they need init . A zero List has no allocator, and push on it returns error.NoAllocator instead of crashing. # Interfaces at the edges Put an interface where your program meets the world: files, the network, the clock, a logger. The logic takes the interface, the program passes the real thing, and a test passes a fake one. No framework is needed. Test output # Do and do not Do Do not defer a.free(x) on the line after the allocation free at the end of the function by hand take str and T[] take List T * when you only read ? to pass errors up catch 0 to make a warning disappear a match that produces a value, without _ , on your own unions a catch-all arm that hides new variants get a pointer into a list late and drop it early keep list.at(i) across a push (the compiler refuses) one arena per unit of work a global allocator that nothing owns +% for hashes + where you expect a wrap (it panics on purpose) comptime assert(sizeof(T) == N) for layouts a comment that says must be 16 bytes defer t.join() or errdefer t.join() right after each spawn a join only at the very end, so that a ? can leave the thread running (the compiler refuses) collect the changes, apply them after the loop list.push(...) inside for (auto x : list) (the compiler refuses) # What next Practice these on small problems: the course . The full list of checks: the safety model . When a message is unclear: debugging .

text: Containers in Zark are ordinary generic structs written in Zark itself (the source is std/std.zk , which is included automatically). title: Interoperating with C and C++

headings.text: Dear ImGui without a C wrapper

text: Zark needs no separate binding layer : a C header is imported like a module, a single C function can be declared in one line, and a C file is passed to the compiler on the command line. This page collects everything you need at the boundary. # Importing a C header import x.h as name; reads a C header and makes its declarations available under name:: . Without as , they land in the importing file's scope. shapes.h shapes.c Output What you get: functions become extern declarations, structs become Zark structs with the same layout, typedef becomes type ; an enum becomes an integer type plus one constant per value; a #define of a number, a string or a character becomes a constant; a union becomes a struct with raw storage and one accessor per member: *u.as_d() = 2.5; ; a static inline function gets a small C wrapper that the compiler builds and links for you; an extern variable becomes a function name_ptr() that returns its address, a struct with bitfields gets get_f() and set_f(v) for each bitfield, and a struct aligned above 8 becomes an align(N) struct (see variables, bitfields and alignment ); a field or parameter named like a Zark keyword gets a trailing _ ( type becomes type_ ). The header is looked up next to the importing file, then in the -I directories, then in the system include path, and it sees the same -D and -I flags as the C sources. The result is cached in .zark-cache/cbind/ and rebuilt when the header, anything it includes, the flags, the clang version or the Zark compiler change. Some C constructs have no Zark equivalent yet and are skipped: long double , _Complex , _Atomic , __int128 , SIMD vector types, function-like macros, thread-local, static and volatile variables, bitfields inside unions, and structs passed by value through function pointer types. import skips them silently; zark cbind lists them. # Seeing the bindings: zark cbind zark cbind prints what an import would produce, plus one warning per skipped declaration: The output is a plain .zk file you can read and edit. With --inline-c the wrappers for static inline functions go to a C file that you compile in next to it ( zark run main.zk shapes_inline.c ). That C file includes the header by its absolute path, and the wrapper names in both files are hashed from that path, so the pair only works on the machine and in the checkout where it was made. Use it to inspect what an import produces, and let import regenerate the bindings elsewhere. A header without static inline functions produces a .zk that does not depend on the path. A header with a C++ extension ( .hpp , .hh , .hxx , .h++ ) is bound as C++, see C++ headers ; a .h file is always read as C. # C++ headers import x.hpp as name; binds a C++ header, and zark cbind x.hpp prints the bindings. A header is C++ when its extension is .hpp , .hh , .hxx or .h++ . clang++ reads the header, and the compiler writes two things: a Zark module and a small C++ file of extern C functions (shims) that make the real calls. Zark never calls a C++ function by its mangled name, and a class never crosses the C boundary by value: classes travel as pointers, and Zark copies the simple ones in and out. The C++ file is compiled and linked for you, and only the shims your program uses are compiled, so a function that the header declares but no file defines is harmless while you do not call it. shapes.hpp shapes.cpp Output How the names come out: In C++ In Zark, under import shapes.hpp as sh; namespace shapes , function dot an empty struct shapes with a static method: sh::shapes::dot(a, b) ; a function outside any namespace is a plain sh::f(x) class shapes::Vec , nested Outer::Inner sh::shapes_Vec , Outer_Inner : the path is joined with _ , types are not nested enum class Kind in shapes , a constexpr constant N sh::shapes_Kind_Box , sh::shapes_N , plain integers method, const method, static method a method of the struct, a const method, a static method: c.get().next() , sh::shapes_Counter::alive() overloaded function one function per overload with a suffix of parameter tokens: scale_f32_f32 , scale_shapes_Vec ( const char* is u8pc , a pointer adds p , a reference pr ); a name that is not overloaded stays as it is default arguments the full name, plus name_k for each shorter call C++ accepts ( k is the number of arguments); C++ fills in the defaults operator+ , == , and the like on a value type Zark operators: a + b , a == b ; an operator with more than one overload on the same type gets no short form, each overload is a method with a parameter suffix ( op_add_i32 , op_add_V ) other operators named methods: op_index for [] , op_call for () , op_add_assign for += , to_bool() for operator bool T , T* T* ; a const T parameter of a number or enum is taken by value, and so is one of a plain value type unless the function returns a reference or a pointer, or something else in the signature (the object the method belongs to, a non-const pointer or reference, a void* ) could reach the same storage; then it stays T* . The by_value manifest key lists value types that are always taken by value static data member, global variable name_ptr() , as for C variables Box int (an instantiated template) Box_i32 std::string , std::string_view in a parameter or result str (a std::string result is copied with an allocator you pass first) std::vector T of numbers or small structs T[] std::unique_ptr T a T_own handle (below) printf-style Text(const char* fmt, ...) Text(u8* fmt) : the text is printed as it is, format it in Zark with bprint Two kinds of classes need different handling: A value type is trivially copyable, like Vec or Dear ImGui's ImVec2 . It is an ordinary Zark struct with the C++ layout, you can copy it, return it and store it, and T{} or T(args) build it. Any other class, like Counter , is non-trivial : it has a destructor, a copy constructor or virtual functions. Zark holds such an object only through a pointer. To make one, call T::create(allocator, args) , which allocates the object

text: Zark is suited to drivers and kernels: device registers are described with structs, privileged instructions are called like ordinary functions, and the program is built without libc. Everything you need is built into the language and the prelude. No macros, no #pragma , no compiler attributes. A field volatile u32 data and a variable volatile u32 x work too. The width of an access always equals the width of the type: volatile u8* reads exactly one byte, volatile u16* two. A packed struct puts the fields back to back, without gaps: this is how descriptors, IDT and GDT tables, packet headers and PCI configuration are laid out. title: Testing

headings.text: Running from an editor and in CI

text: Tests are built into the language: a special test block is written next to the code, and the command zark test runs them. No separate libraries or configuration files are needed. # The first test Test output Run it with the command: test name { ... } is a top-level declaration. Inside is ordinary code. A test is a function that returns !void , so ? works in it. A test passes if the block reaches its end. It fails if an assert or panic fires, or if ? receives an error. # What zark test does Compiles the file with all the test blocks (and with all its imports). Runs each test in a separate process . The failure of one (even a crash) does not break the others. Prints ok or FAIL for each and a summary. For failed tests, shows everything they printed. Returns exit code 0 if nothing failed, and 1 if something did. test blocks are ignored by zark run and zark build . A file with tests remains an ordinary program. # What failures look like Test output Each failure shows its reason: error: Name : ? propagated an error; assertion failed (file:line) : the condition in assert is false; panic: message (file:line) : panic was called. The output of passed tests is hidden: it is needed only when something is broken. # assert assert(condition) checks a bool . If the condition is false, the program ends with a message and a location. It works not only in tests but in ordinary code too: Output exit code 1 assert has no separate message. If you need context, use panic with a format: Output exit code 1 # Testing errors An expected error is checked with catch : Test output The pattern is this: catch |e| checks the error and leaves the test through return . If there was no error, control reaches assert(false) and the test fails. # Testing with memory Tests can allocate memory like ordinary code. Create an allocator inside the test and free through defer : Test output The last test shows the advantage of explicit allocators: the behavior when memory runs out is checked deterministically, with no hacks. # Organization Tests are usually written in the same file , under the code they check: then nothing needs to be imported. If there are many tests, create a separate file and import the module: mathx.zk Test output Only the tests of the file you specified are run. The test blocks of imported files are not run. Test names may repeat (the compiler does not check), but it is better if they are unique: you find the failed test by its name. # A file without tests If a file has no test blocks at all, the command reports 0 passed, 0 failed and exits with code 0. Do not confuse this with all tests passed . # Running from an editor and in CI In VS Code / code-oss the extension shows a run button above every test (see tooling ). In CI one command is enough: zark test main.zk . Exit code 1 means a failure. The optimization mode can be switched: zark test main.zk -O runs the same tests through LLVM -O2 . Useful for making sure optimizations do not change the behavior. # What next Failing tests often come down to errors: errors and optional values . How the compiler's own test suite is organized: how it all works .

title: Tools: fmt, lsp, flags
text: All the tools are subcommands of one executable, zark . Nothing separate needs to be installed. # Compiler diagnostics Every error is printed in the form file:line: error: message , and under it the source line is shown with a ^ pointing at the place of the error: Compiler output When the program has a similar name, the compiler suggests it (for names shorter than three characters no suggestions are shown, they would be random): an unknown variable or function; a struct field, an enum or union variant, a name in a closure's capture list; the name of a generic constraint ( T: Orb → Ord ). Typical messages and their causes are explained on the page pitfalls and FAQ . Note: the compiler stops at the first parser error. It also reports type errors one per run, but the language server checks every function separately and shows one error per function. # zark fmt zark fmt file.zk ... rewrites files in place. The formatter works on tokens: it fixes spaces, indentation and blank lines, never wraps or joins lines and does not touch comments. What exactly the formatter does: indentation is 4 spaces per level of bracket nesting; a continuation of an expression on the next line gets one more level; spaces around binary operators, after commas and colons, inside { } on one line; no spaces inside () and [] ; the angle brackets of generics ( List i64 ) stay as written; runs of blank lines collapse into one, and blank lines right after { and before } are removed; trailing spaces are removed, and the file ends with exactly one newline; the distance between code and a trailing comment is kept as it is. What the formatter does not do: it does not break long lines, does not align comments to a column, does not reorder declarations, does not rename anything. Spaces around * and , when the neighboring tokens do not show whether it is multiplication or a pointer ( i*2 in the example above), are left as they were. --check changes nothing and prints would reformat file for every file that would be changed, and exits with code 1: handy for CI: The formatter is idempotent: running it again on an already formatted file changes nothing. It is guaranteed to preserve the stream of tokens: the meaning of the program cannot change. Note: files with \r\n line endings are turned into \n by the formatter. # Compilation modes Zark has two backends: the own x86-64 backend (the default). The compiler itself turns the intermediate representation into machine code and writes an ELF object. The build is very fast; the code is noticeably faster than naive code because there is register allocation, but slower than optimized LLVM; LLVM ( --llvm , -O , --release ): the compiler prints LLVM IR, and clang optimizes and compiles it. Command Backend Optimization Bounds checks zark run x.zk own none yes zark run x.zk --llvm LLVM -O0 yes zark run x.zk -O LLVM -O2 yes zark run x.zk --release LLVM -O2 no zark run x.zk --no-safety own none no The bounds check is what turns going out of an array into a clear panic. Without it this is undefined behavior : the example below fails with a panic in a normal build and silently reads garbage with --release : ( oob.zk reads a[5] of an array of three elements.) Keep debug builds with the checks, and turn on --release for finished programs when you are sure the indexes are correct. For development use the default mode: it builds the compiler itself (about 25 thousand lines of Zark) in about a third of a second, not counting the link. # Intermediate representations zark ir file.zk prints the LLVM IR that the frontend generated. It is the same text that the own backend reads. For the function you get (local variables live in alloca , the names %tN are temporary values): zark tokens file.zk prints the tokens: the line number, the kind of the token and the text. Useful when it is unclear how the lexer split a line (especially with quotes and curly braces): How everything else works is on the page how the compiler works . # Language server and editor zark lsp is a language server over the LSP protocol on standard input/output. It is built on the same parser and generator as the compiler, so the messages are the same as with zark build , and they also apply to unsaved changes. Features: Feature What it can do Diagnostics errors with an exact range as you type, did you mean hints, quick fixes Hover the signature of a symbol and the /// comments above the declaration Completion struct members and methods (by the inferred type) after . , - and :: , module names after alias:: , enum variants after . , literal fields after . inside Name{ ... } , local variables, global names, keywords Parameter hints when typing ( and , : the signature of the function or method being called Go to definition including into imported files and by the path inside import ... References and rename across the whole working directory, including the files that import your file File outline a tree of structs, enums, functions, methods and tests Symbol search Ctrl+T over all the .zk files of the working directory Occurrence highlighting all the uses of the symbol under the cursor Formatting the same as zark fmt Note: diagnostics work like this: the server runs the compiler's frontend on every function of the file (except generic ones, which are checked only when they are called) and collects one error per function. The parser stops at the first syntax error in a file. What the server does not do: it does not show the types of expressions, cannot refactor except for renaming, and does not infer types in complex generic expressions (there are simply no hints there). # VS Code and code-oss The repository contains the extension editors/vscode . It starts zark lsp and adds syntax highlighting, snippets, run and test buttons, and the command Zark: Restart Language Server . After installing, reload the window ( Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window ) and open any .zk file. Settings: Setting Value zark.path the path to zark ; by default i

title: Projects and dependencies
text: A single file is enough to start. When a program grows into several files, C code or other people's libraries, describe it in a zark.toml and zark run , zark build and zark test work without a file name. The commands find zark.toml in the current directory or any directory above it, so they also work from src/sub/ . A file named on the command line ( zark run tools/gen.zk ) inside a project still gets the project's dependencies, C sources and libraries. # zark.toml The format is a small part of TOML: sections, key = value , strings, integers, booleans, lists and inline tables, and # comments. A mistake is reported with the line: zark.toml:2: error: unterminated string . # Dependencies A dependency is imported by its name: path dependencies point to a directory on disk. git dependencies are cloned into .zark/deps/NAME the first time a command needs them ( rev is a tag or branch). Delete the directory to fetch again. A dependency with its own zark.toml brings its own dependencies, C sources and libraries along. Without a manifest, its lib file is src/lib.zk or lib.zk . Imports that start with ./ or ../ are always relative files, so a dependency name never hides them. The language server reads the same manifest, so imports of dependencies are found in the editor too.

title: Standard modules
text: Besides the prelude, which every program gets automatically, the standard library has modules that you import by name. They are built into the compiler, so there is nothing to install: Always give a module a name with as : its functions are then written fs::list_dir(...) and do not mix with your own names. Module What is in it std/fs file metadata, directories, walking a tree, copying, moving, removing, temporary directories std/path path strings: join , base , dir , ext , stem , normalize , relative , absolute std/time wall clock, DateTime with time zones, parsing and printing ISO 8601, Stopwatch , sleep_ms std/os running programs and capturing their output, environment variables, cpu_count , exe_path std/args command-line options with --help std/json JSON parsing with error positions, a tree you can query and build, and a streaming Builder std/net TCP sockets and DNS (see networking and threads ) std/http an HTTP/1.1 client and a small server std/thread threads, Mutex , Cond , WaitGroup , Channel T Like everything in Zark, nothing here allocates on its own: functions that return new strings or lists take an Allocator , and the results have a deinit() or are freed with that allocator. # std/fs Output Function What it does info(p) , link_info(p) Info{ kind, size, modified, mode } ; kind is .File , .Dir , .Link or .Other exists , is_dir , is_file list_dir(a, p) a DirList sorted by name: for (auto e : d.slice()) { e.name; e.kind } walk(a, root) , walk_all(a, root) every file below root (with directories for walk_all ), as relative paths make_dir , make_dirs one directory, or with every missing parent remove_file , remove_dir , remove_all(a, p) move(from, to) , copy_file(from, to) , append_file(p, data) , set_mode(p, mode) cwd(a) , set_cwd(p) , temp_dir(a, prefix) Errors are the usual names: error.NotFound , error.PermissionDenied , error.AlreadyExists , error.DirectoryNotEmpty , error.NotADirectory . Whole files are read and written with the prelude's read_file and write_file . # std/path Output # std/time Output DateTime has the fields year, month, day, hour, minute, second, nsec, offset (seconds east of UTC) and prints itself as ISO 8601. now_utc() , now_local() , utc(t) , local(t) and from_unix(t, offset) make one; parse reads 2026-11-20 , 2026-11-20T10:43 , ...:05.250Z and ...+01:00 . unix() , unix_ms() and mono_ns() read the clocks. # std/os Output exec finds the program through PATH , waits for it and returns Output{ code, out, err } ; a program that does not exist gives error.ProgramNotFound . exec_with also takes cwd and input (written to the program's stdin). shell(a, cmd | cmd ) runs a line through /bin/sh . The rest: set_env , unset_env , env_or(name, default) , pid() , exit(code) , exe_path(a) , args(a) , cpu_count() . # std/args Output In a real program call p.parse() , which reads the process arguments. --help (or -h ) prints the usage and makes parse return error.Help ; a wrong option prints a message and returns error.UnknownOption or error.MissingValue . Accepted forms: --name , --name=value , --name value , -n value , -nvalue , combined flags -abc , and -- before arguments that start with - . # std/json Output Reading: get(key) and at(i) never fail; a missing member is a null value, so you can write chains. as_str , as_i64 , as_f64 , as_bool return an error when the type differs; str_or , int_or , f64_or , bool_or take a default. items() and members() iterate. Integers are read from the literal, so as_i64 is exact beyond 2^53. Strings without escapes point into the input text: keep it alive as long as the tree. Printing: println(*v) gives compact JSON, {*v:p} indented; stringify(a, v, pretty) returns a string. Building: object , array , string , number , integer , boolean , null_value , then set(key, v) and push(v) . Builder writes JSON straight into a List u8 without a tree: begin_object , key , string , integer , number , boolean , null_value , value(tree) , end . Use an Arena for a parsed tree: everything is freed at once with deinit() . # What next Networking and threads : std/net , std/http and std/thread . Standard library reference : the prelude.

title: Networking and threads
text: # std/thread Output spawn runs a closure on a new thread. The closure keeps pointers to what it captures, so join every thread before those variables go out of scope . spawn_fn(f, arg) starts a plain fn(void*) instead. The compiler checks the part of this rule that it can see. A Thread in a variable has to be joined (or detached, or handed on to something else) on every path out of the function, including the path that a ? takes when it fails. A thread that is dropped on the spot is refused, and so is returning a thread whose closure captured a local variable of the function: Compiler output If work() fails, main would return while the thread still uses hits . The fix is the same as for memory: put the cleanup next to the creation. defer runs on every way out; errdefer only on the failing ones, so the normal path can still join where it wants to: Output When a worker waits for work (a channel, a server), joining it on the error path would wait forever, so stop it first. Put the stop and the join in one defer or errdefer block, in that order, or use a block so that the threads' lifetime is the lifetime of the block, as in the channel example above. What the compiler does not see: threads kept in a list or an array (join them in a loop, as above), data races, and the order of joins. See the safety model . Type What it is Thread join() , detach() Mutex lock() , unlock() , try_lock() ; the zero value is ready Cond wait( m) , wait_ms( m, ms) , signal() , broadcast() AtomicI64 add(d) (returns the old value), load() , store(x) , compare_swap(old, new) WaitGroup add(n) , done() , wait() Channel T a bounded queue: Channel T ::create(a, capacity) , send(v) , recv() , try_recv() , close() , destroy() parallel_for(n, threads, body) calls body(i) for every i in 0..n , split over threads threads (0 means one per CPU), and returns when all are done. Locks, channels and wait groups must not be copied once used: share them through a pointer (a channel is created on the heap for that reason). Output # std/net Output listen(host, port) gives a Listener with accept() , port() and close() (which also wakes up a thread blocked in accept ). connect_to(host, port) gives a Conn : read(buf) (0 at the end), write_all(s) , print(...) with interpolation and no allocation, set_timeout(ms) , close_write() , close() , peer(buf) . Reader::init( conn, buf) buffers reads: read_line() , read_exact( list, n) , read_all( list) . Errors: error.HostNotFound , error.ConnectionRefused , error.AddressInUse , error.TimedOut , error.ConnectionReset . # std/http The client speaks HTTP/1.1 over http:// and https:// . HTTPS uses the system's OpenSSL library ( libssl.so.3 ), loaded the first time it is needed, so programs need no extra link flags; certificates and host names are checked against the system store. Request fields: method ( GET ), url , headers , body , timeout_ms (30000), max_redirects (5), insecure (skip certificate checks), ca_file (trust these PEM certificates instead of the system store). Reply : status , reason , headers , body , header(name) (case-insensitive), ok() , deinit() . Chunked bodies and redirects are handled. Errors: error.UnsupportedScheme , error.InvalidUrl , error.CertificateInvalid , error.TlsUnavailable (no libssl), plus the network errors above. url_encode(a, s) , url_decode(a, s) , parse_url(s) . The server runs a handler on a pool of threads, keeps connections alive and gives every request its own arena: Output ServerRequest : method , path , query , headers , body , peer , header(name) , param(name) (decoded query parameter), and a , an allocator freed after the handler returns. ServerResponse : set status (200), header(name, value) , then exactly one of text , html , json , send(content_type, body) or printf(content_type, ...) . serve(a, threads, handler) blocks until stop() . The handler runs on several threads at once: guard shared data with a Mutex or use atomics. The server speaks plain HTTP; put it behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) for HTTPS.

text: This page collects what is not obvious: places where you can make a mistake and places where Zark works differently from the languages you are used to. Every pitfall has an example. If you got a strange result or an error, look here. # Numbers # A literal must fit its type Compiler output const u8 b = 300; and const u32 x = -1; are compile errors. A value computed at run time that does not fit is an overflow panic (see below). # Integer overflow is a panic Output exit code 1 In a safe build the program stops with panic: integer overflow and the file and line. If wrapping is what you want, write +% , -% or *% ; otherwise compute in a wider type. --release removes the check and the result wraps around. # Integer division by zero panics Output exit code 1 It is a panic, not an error : it cannot be caught with catch , and the message has the file and line. Check the divisor before dividing. In --release the check is removed. # / on integers drops the fraction 7 / 2 is 3 , and -7 / 2 is -3 (towards zero). For a fractional result convert: 7 as f64 / 2 as f64 . # Floating-point literals hide imprecision 0.1 + 0.2 is printed as 0.3 because the output goes through %g . But 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false . Compare floats with a tolerance. # Narrowing and a change of sign only through as const i32 small = big; will not compile. This is deliberate: Conversions are visible . # 300 as u8 from a literal A literal in as is handled as a constant and may not be truncated. To check the behavior, put the number in a variable: auto n = 300; n as u8 gives 44. # Strings # { in a string opens an interpolation Output The compiler took { key ... for an interpolation of the string key , and instead of JSON you got an unexpected output. Write a literal brace as {{ and }} : Output # Interpolation works only in print functions const auto s = n = {n} ; is an error. Build a string value with bprint or sprint (see strings ). # You cannot modify a literal Output exit code 1 Writing into a literal crashes the program. Copy into a buffer. # str is bytes, not characters привет .len is 12 , not 6 . Indexing gives bytes. For ASCII everything is simple; for other scripts you have to parse UTF-8 by hand. # A slice of a string does not end with a zero byte puts(s[0..2].ptr) will print the whole original string. For C use to_cstr or dupz (see C ). # There is no + for strings Joining is done with str_join , str_concat , bprint or sprint ; there are also str_split , str_replace and str_to_upper (see the reference ). They take an Allocator because the result is a new string. # A wrong format is printed as bad format The specification is checked when printing, not at compile time. An unknown letter ( {n:b} ) or a format that does not suit the type gives bad format in the output, and the program goes on. # There is no binary output The format {n:b} is not supported: the allowed ones for integers are d , i , u , x , X , o , c . # Variables and scopes # A parameter is a copy Output Parameters and variables are mutable, but the function changes its own copy. To forbid changing a parameter, write const i64 x . To change the caller's data, pass a pointer. # The same name twice in one block Compiler output In a nested block you can shadow, in the same one you cannot. # A variable hides a function const auto max = 5; makes the call max(1, 2) impossible in that block. # The names from the prelude are taken You cannot declare functions max , min , abs , sort , swap , run , env , arg , cstr : duplicate function . Choose other names. # A global array requires an initializer i64[3] arr; at the top level without = ... does not compile. Write i64[3] arr = [0, 0, 0]; . # A const with a function call is evaluated every time const auto K = next(); at the top level is a substitution of the expression, and the side effect fires at every use. # Control flow # A forgotten ; Every statement ends with ; . Without it the compiler stops at the next token: Compiler output # if is not an expression auto x = if (a) { 1 } else { 2 }; is an error. Use match ( match a { true = 1, false = 2 } ) or a variable declared in advance. # In a catch block an expression must come last A block that ends with a match or if as a statement does not count as a value. Put the result in a variable and make it the last line. # The condition must be bool if (n) and while (p) do not work. Write n != 0 and p != null . # No 0..=n , a, b = b, a , x++ as an expression This is deliberate: one form per action. x++ and the compound assignments ( += -= *= /= %= |= = ^= = = ) exist, but only as statements. # break and continue name a loop through a label To leave an outer loop, label it ( outer: for (...) ) and write break outer; . Without a label they affect the nearest loop. # A match statement on an integer, string or pointer does not have to be complete If no pattern fits, nothing happens. A match on an enum or union is exhaustive in a statement too, and a match expression needs _ for the other types. # A function must return a value on every path Compiler output The compiler checks that a function with a result never falls off its end. A path returns when it ends in return , an if with an else where both branches return, a match where every arm returns, an endless while (true) without a break , or a call to panic . # Errors and optional values # catch and orelse take everything to the right f(5) catch 0 + 100 is f(5) catch (0 + 100) , the result is 5 , not 105 . Use parentheses: (f(5) catch 0) + 100 . # ? only in a function with !T In an ordinary function ? is not allowed: there is nowhere to propagate to. # You cannot ignore a !T f() without ? , catch or _ = does not compile. # ?T is not compared with null For ?T use orelse , is .None , match . Only ordinary pointers can be compared with null . # catch return) in parentheses In a call argument, catch return before the closing parenthesis is not parsed. text: Most of the time with a new language goes into reading what it tells you. This page teaches that: how a message is built, the messages you will meet most often with the fix for each, and what to do when the program compiles and still does the wrong thing. # How an error message is built Compiler output Where: file and line, then the severity. What: one sentence. Names in single quotes are names from your code. The line itself , and under it a caret ^ at the expression the message is about. A suggestion when the compiler can guess ( did you mean ... ). Read the first message first. The compiler stops a function at its first problem, so later messages often disappear once the first is fixed. # Common compile errors and their fixes A type does not fit. The compiler does not narrow or change sign by itself: Compiler output Fix: write big as i32 if losing bits is acceptable, or use the wider type. A function does not always return: Compiler output Fix: add the return 0; for the remaining case. A forgotten error: Compiler output Fix: parse( 12 )? in a function that returns !T , catch with a fallback, or _ = parse( 12 ) catch 0; if you really want to ignore it. A match that is missing a case: Compiler output Fix: add .West (this is the check that makes adding a variant safe). A struct that does not satisfy an interface: Compiler output Fix: implement the missing method. A string with braces: Compiler output Fix: a literal brace is written twice, {{\ a\ : 1, \ b\ : 2}} . Interpolation is {expression} or {expression:format} . # Ownership messages These come from the checks described in the safety model . They always name two lines: where the thing stopped being valid, and where you used it. Compiler output 'buf' is used after 'free' consumed it : the line above is the free . Either remove the later use, move the free to after the last use, or give the variable a new value first. Compiler output 'view' points into 'l', and 'push' ... may have moved or freed that memory : take view again after the push . Compiler output returning something that points into local : the local dies when the function returns. Return the value, let the caller pass in the storage, or allocate with an allocator. # What a panic tells you A panic is a bug in the program. The message has the reason and the place: Message Meaning Look for index 3 out of bounds (len 3) an index past the end an off-by-one, a loop to len instead of len - 1 slice [2..9] out of bounds (len 5) a slice range that does not fit the arithmetic of the range division by zero a divisor that is zero a missing check before / or % integer overflow a result that does not fit its type a type that is too small, or +% was meant assertion failed an assert that was false the condition and the data that reached it Run the failing case again under -g and gdb to see the variables. -g adds line numbers, local variables, structs and arrays to the debug information. Breakpoints by file:line work. # The program is wrong but nothing fails Print the data. println prints a struct with its field names and a slice with its elements. Print before and after the step you suspect. Write a test that fails. Put the smallest input that shows the problem in a test block, run zark test file.zk , and fix until it is green. The test stays as protection. Shrink the input. Remove code and data until the problem is still there and nothing else is. The cause is usually visible at that point. Ask a different backend. zark run file.zk , then zark run file.zk --llvm and -O . In the safe mode all of them must print the same. If they do not, you have found a compiler bug; save the file. # Memory problems If the program crashes with a segmentation fault, or a result changes from run to run, assume memory first. Run it with the crash handler (it is on by default). The reason line says null pointer , stack overflow or use after free . Change the allocator in the failing path to a DebugAllocator ( DebugAllocator::init() and dbg.allocator() ). A use after free, even through a copy, stops at the exact access and names the block. dbg.deinit()? reports blocks that were never freed. If a block number is reported, set dbg.trap_id to it and run under gdb : the program stops where the block was allocated. # When it is slow That is the compiler's time. For the program's own, build with -O (optimized and still safe). If it is still too slow and tested, --release removes the checks. Measure before and after: do not guess. # Looking inside the compiler Command Shows zark tokens file.zk the tokens after the lexer zark ir file.zk the LLVM IR that the compiler generates zark fmt file.zk nothing: it rewrites the file with the standard formatting (use --check to only test) When you report a compiler bug, include the smallest file that shows it, the command you ran, and the output. # What next The list of what is checked: the safety model . The questions that people ask first: pitfalls and FAQ .

title: How it all works
text: This page is for those who want to understand what happens under the hood, or who are going to change the compiler. It is not required for writing programs. # The pipeline The compiler is a program in Zark itself, about 12 thousand lines in the selfhost/ directory. It works as a pipeline: What each file does: File Role lexer.zk tokens (see lexical structure ) ast.zk fat tree nodes with a kind tag parser.zk parsing the syntax, splitting {x} into parts gen.zk types, instantiating generics, functions, diagnostics gen_stmt.zk statements, defer / errdefer , match gen_expr.zk expressions, addresses, operators, casts gen_call.zk calls, inferring type parameters, methods, function pointers gen_fmt.zk building Fmt for calls with interpolation, panic , assert , embed resolve.zk , loader.zk imports and module prefixes native.zk the own backend: IR → x86-64 (System V ABI), register allocation x64.zk the instruction encoder and the ELF64 object writer fmt.zk the zark fmt formatter lsp.zk , ide.zk , analysis.zk , json.zk , textpos.zk the language server diag.zk nice error messages, did you mean main.zk the command-line driver You can see the intermediate results right from the CLI: zark tokens file.zk (tokens) and zark ir file.zk (LLVM IR). More in tooling . The prelude ( std/std.zk ) is built into the compiler through embed , so zark is one executable without external data. # Two backends The own one (default). It parses the textual LLVM IR that the frontend generated and turns it into x86-64 machine code. It uses linear-scan register allocation, fusing a comparison with a branch, constants in operands, and lazy loading of composite values. There is not a single line of LLVM inside. The purpose is a fast build: a typical project builds in fractions of a second. LLVM ( -O , --release , --llvm ). The same IR is handed to clang , which does full optimization. It is needed for speed in production builds. A comparison for a program of 10 thousand lines, from source to executable (the author's measurements): Builder Time zark, own backend, safe mode (bounds, division and overflow checks) about 200 ms zark, own backend, --no-safety about 135 ms clang -O0 about 315 ms gcc -O0 about 710 ms And the speed of the result (recursive fib(38) and a sieve of 50 million): fib(38) sieve 50M C ( clang -O2 ) 90 ms 560 ms Zark --release (no checks) 100 ms 575 ms Zark -O (all checks on) 170 ms 540 ms C ( clang -O0 ) 250 ms 780 ms Zark, own backend (safe mode) about 360 ms about 1210 ms So --release does not lose to C, -O keeps every check for a small price, and the default build wins in compile speed. The checks cost most in the own backend, which does not optimize them away. # Self-hosting and the fixed point The compiler builds itself. To start from zero, the repository holds a seed : the LLVM IR of the compiler itself ( bootstrap/seed.ll.gz ). clang turns it into the first working compiler. The check: stage2 and stage3 are identical byte for byte (the fixed point). The same is done for the chain with the own backend without LLVM (native2 == native3). The script bootstrap.sh runs everything, then runs the test suite and puts the result into build/zark . A consequence for development: a new language feature is added in two steps. First the compiler is taught the feature without using it in its own sources, and the seed is updated ( tools/update-seed.sh ). Only then can the feature be used in selfhost/ : otherwise the old seed cannot build the new code. # The memory layout of types The principle what you see is what is in memory : Type In memory i8..i64 , u8..u64 an integer of the corresponding size bool one byte T* a pointer, 8 bytes T[] , str { ptr, len } , 16 bytes T[N] N elements in a row struct the fields in order, alignment as in C enum a 32-bit integer union { i32 tag, payload } , the payload sized for the largest variant !T { i32 error code, T } fn(A) - R a function pointer fn[](A) - R a pair: a function pointer and a context pointer This explains why structs can be passed to C (by pointer), why nothing needs to be packed at a call and why sizeof is predictable. # How interpolation is expanded The compiler knows neither print nor println . It knows one rule: if the last parameter of the called function has the type Fmt (declared in std/std.zk ), all the remaining arguments and strings with {...} are gathered into a Fmt value. Fmt is a list of pieces: literal text, a pointer to a value, a function that knows how to print a value of that type, and a specification ( :08X , :.2 and so on). The print functions for structs, enums, unions and arrays are generated by the compiler from the type as ordinary Zark code. For numbers, strings and pointers the functions from the prelude are used ( __fmt_int , __fmt_str and others). Everything lies on the caller's stack, and nothing is allocated on the heap. So interpolation is allowed where there is a function with a Fmt parameter: print , println , eprint , eprintln , panic , bprint , sprint and your own. # How generics work Functions and structs with type parameters are monomorphized : for each combination of arguments the compiler creates a separate copy. So there is no run-time overhead. The body of a generic is checked at its declaration against the declared constraints ( T: Ord ); a call with a type that does not satisfy the constraint is reported at the call. A generic without a constraint is checked when it is instantiated. # How defer and errdefer work The compiler expands defer into code on every path out of the block: before return , break , continue and at the end of the block. For errdefer the code is added only on the paths where an error is returned. There is no run-time machinery for this. # How ? and catch work f()? turns into a check of the error code: if it is not zero, defer and errdefer run and the same !T is returned. catch is the same check, but instead of returning it takes the branch with the fallback value. # Lazy compilation Only the functions

title: Cheat sheet
text: A short memo. Details on each topic are behind the links. # A program Output Command What it does zark run f.zk [-- args] build and run zark build f.zk [-o out] [--release] build an executable zark test f.zk run the test blocks zark fmt [--check] f.zk format zark lsp the language server zark ir f.zk show the LLVM IR See installation and tooling . # Lexical structure comments // line , /* block */ end of a statement ; (not needed after the } of a block) numbers 42 , 0xff , 0b101 , 0o17 , 1_000 , 3.14 , 1e9 character 'a' is a u8 number strings text , escapes \n \t \r \0 \e \\ \ \' \{ \} interpolation x = {expr} , literal braces {{ }} See lexical structure . # Types integers i8 i16 i32 i64 isize , u8 u16 u32 u64 usize floating-point f32 f64 other bool , void , str (= u8[] ) pointer T* , void* , null slice / array T[] , T[N] error / optional !T , ?T functions fn(A, B) - R , closure fn[](A) - R alias type Name = Type; SIMD f32x4 , i32x8 , u8x16 : f32x4(a, b, c, d) , f32x4(x) , v[i] See types . # Variables Output A variable is mutable, const makes it immutable, auto infers the type, and without a value it is zero. See testing . # Pitfalls in one line A literal outside the range of its type is a compile error, and integer overflow is a panic in a safe build (use +% , -% , *% to wrap on purpose; --release removes the check). Integer division by zero is a panic (in --release it is not checked). catch and orelse take everything to the right: use parentheses. { in a string is an interpolation, a literal brace is {{ . A closure must not outlive the variables it captures; a function without a return on every path does not compile. The prelude names ( min , max , abs , sort , run , env ) are taken.
